choices: Clarification
Facilitation
Interpretation
Reflection
questions.explanation: Encouraging the patient to keep talking and provide more information — open prompts, nodding, not interrupting — is facilitation. Clarification, reflection, and interpretation each work with what the patient has already said rather than drawing more out of him.
questions.question: You are kneeling next to a 17-year-old with a gunshot wound to his left upper leg, and he is screaming in pain. As you control the bleeding, you say, "Go on — tell me more about what happened," and you nod and keep eye contact while he talks so he will keep giving you information. Which therapeutic communication technique are you using?

choices: Establishing your authority as the emergency responder in charge
Calling for additional resources before you talk to anyone
Considering the perspective of the other person
Exerting your influence to move the situation forward as fast as possible
questions.explanation: In a crisis, people hear and respond through their own fear and stress, so effective communication starts with considering the other person's perspective. Taking over, pushing harder, or avoiding the conversation does not get you the information or cooperation you need.
questions.question: The scene of the shooting is chaotic: witnesses are upset, officers are trying to interview people, and a distraught bystander keeps shouting over everyone. You need information from the people on scene. When communicating in a crisis like this, what matters most?

choices: Use open prompts, reflect and clarify what she tells you, show empathy, and pause to let her answer
Ask a rapid series of yes-or-no questions so the interview stays short
Confront her right away about anything in her story that does not add up
Do most of the talking yourself, explaining procedures in detail so she does not have to speak
questions.explanation: Facilitation, reflection, clarification, and interpretation — backed by empathy and pausing to listen — are the techniques that draw a complete history out of a patient. Leading or confrontational approaches and one-sided talking shut information down instead of gathering it.
questions.question: Your BLS unit is caring for an 86-year-old woman who fell into her bathtub around 3 AM and could not get out until a hospice worker found her at 10 AM. She is alert and has been able to rate her hip and back pain. You want the fullest possible account of what happened from her. Which approach best fits that goal?

choices: "Can you walk me through what happened tonight?"
"Where does it hurt the most right now?"
"Is there anything else you want me to know?"
"He shot you because of his sister, didn't he?"
questions.explanation: The last question is leading and biased — it hands the patient a version of events and pushes him to agree with it, which contaminates his account. The other questions are open or neutral and let him describe the injury in his own words.
questions.question: You are interviewing the 17-year-old shooting patient about how he was injured. Which of the following questions should you avoid asking him?

choices: Ask law enforcement to take him into custody so he has to go
Contact medical control
Immediately stop patient care and leave the scene
Find another person on scene to continue his medical care
questions.explanation: A refusal is not a cue to abandon the patient or hand him to police or bystanders. Contacting medical control gets a physician involved in the refusal, which protects the patient and guides what you do next.
questions.question: The bleeding from the teenager's leg wound is controlled, his vitals are pulse 96, respirations 22, blood pressure 104/76, and SpO2 98% on room air — but now he tells you he refuses to be transported to the hospital. What should you do?

choices: Provide as much detail as possible, including the names you overheard and the story about the shooter's sister
Use code words so nobody listening can figure out what happened
Stay objective and impartial — report the wound, the vitals, and your treatment, not your theory of the shooting
Speak as quickly and loudly as possible so the hospital copies every word
questions.explanation: A radio report is a clinical handoff, not a police narrative: it stays objective and impartial, covering the patient's condition and care. Broadcasting names and speculation about the crime is not part of the patient's medical report.
questions.question: As you radio the hospital with a report on the shooting patient, the officers are still sorting out who shot him and why. Which approach to that radio report is correct?
questions.topic: Radio reports and the receiving hospital

choices: The patient's full name and date of birth
The address of the apartment complex you are coming from
Your personal opinion of the patient's condition
Your estimated time of arrival
questions.explanation: The initial report gives the hospital what it needs to get ready — the patient's presentation and your estimated time of arrival. Names, the scene address, and personal opinions are not part of that initial notification.
questions.question: You are giving your initial report to the hospital on the 17-year-old gunshot patient. Which piece of information belongs in that initial report?
questions.topic: Radio reports and the receiving hospital

choices: What category does this patient fit into?
What got us to this point in care?
What are the future possible options?
How often does a situation like this occur?
questions.explanation: A shared mental model is built first on a common understanding of what has already happened — what got the patient and the team to this point in care. Future options only make sense once everyone shares that starting picture.
questions.question: During the handoff of the shooting patient, you want your crew and the hospital team working from the same shared picture of the call — the same mental model. Building that mental model starts with answering which question?
questions.topic: Radio reports and the receiving hospital

choices: It lets the hospital know her chief complaint and condition so staff can prepare equipment or gather specialized help if she needs it
It takes the place of the written patient care report for the call
It is mainly how the hospital collects demographic information for billing
You are required to get the hospital's permission before you can transport her
questions.explanation: The prearrival report notifies the hospital of the patient's chief complaint and condition — here, possible traumatic injury and hypothermia in an older woman — so the staff can have equipment or additional treatment support ready when she arrives. It never replaces the written report.
questions.question: Before you transport the 86-year-old woman who spent about seven hours in her bathtub, you give the receiving hospital a prearrival radio report. What is the primary reason for giving that report?
questions.topic: Radio reports and the receiving hospital

choices: "What is your estimated time of arrival?"
"Does she have any medical history?"
"Did she lose consciousness at any point, and what is her pain level now?"
"What were her vital signs?"
questions.explanation: Your ETA, her diabetes history, and her vital signs were already in your report, so the ED has those. What they still need — and typically ask for — is whether she lost consciousness, her pain level, and similar gaps in the information you gave.
questions.question: You radio Columbus Community Hospital: an alert 86-year-old woman, fell into her tub at 3 AM and was found at 10 AM, pale and cold skin, crepitus in the pelvic girdle, BP 112/84, pulse 72, respirations 14, immobilized with a c-collar, pulse/motor/sensory intact in all four extremities, history of diabetes, ETA 10 minutes. Which question should you anticipate the emergency department asking you back?
questions.topic: Radio reports and the receiving hospital

choices: Diabetes means she cannot feel pain at all, so her pain ratings can be ignored
Diabetes only matters later, once the hospital starts choosing medications
A pain rating of 10 rules out any glucose problem as a cause of her fall
High or low blood glucose may have played a role in her fall, and diabetes can blunt or heighten pain perception, so her reported pain may not match the severity of her injuries
questions.explanation: Checking her glucose, if permitted, matters because abnormal glucose may have contributed to the fall. And because high glucose affects nerve endings, diabetes can decrease pain perception in some patients or markedly increase it through neuropathy — so her ratings have to be interpreted with that in mind and her diabetes status communicated to the hospital.
questions.question: The woman in the bathtub rates her back pain an 8 and her hip pain a 10, and she has a history of diabetes. Why does her diabetes matter to how the team interprets this call and what you communicate about it?
questions.topic: Radio reports and the receiving hospital

choices: Your opinions about why the patient was shot
As many abbreviations as you can fit into the text
The address of the apartment complex
Your physical assessment findings
questions.explanation: The narrative documents the clinical picture — your physical assessment findings such as the wound, vitals, and skin signs. Opinions about the shooting do not belong in a patient care document.
questions.question: You are writing the narrative for the gunshot call. Which of the following belongs in that narrative?

choices: Follow your agency's directions for making an amendment to the report
Leave the record as it is and seek legal advice
Notify the information technology department and have the report deleted
Say nothing and hope the error goes unnoticed
questions.explanation: Errors in a submitted record are corrected through your agency's amendment process, which preserves the original entry and documents the change. Leaving wrong vitals in place, deleting the report, or staying silent all leave a false medical record.
questions.question: After you submit the electronic PCR for the gunshot call, you realize you accidentally documented the wrong vital signs. What should you do?

choices: Internet laws
NEMSIS
HIPAA
Patient care report protocol
questions.explanation: Photos of an identifiable patient are protected health information. Sharing them outside of care is a violation of HIPAA, the federal law governing patient privacy.
questions.question: On the way back from the shooting call, your partner shows you several photos he took of the patient and the scene, which he plans to post online to share with friends. Posting those photos could be a violation of:

choices: Check boxes are not permitted on calls involving trauma
The narrative tells the story of the call — the events leading up to it, the scene, the progression of symptoms, and her response to treatment — with a level of detail check boxes cannot provide
A narrative is faster to complete than a set of check boxes
Writing a narrative means the recorded vital signs do not need to be exact
questions.explanation: Check boxes are quick and consistent, but they leave no room for explanatory detail or the history of the call. The narrative carries the story — how she fell, seven hours in the tub, her findings and how they evolved — which is what the next caregivers need.
questions.question: Your PCR form has check boxes that capture vitals and demographics quickly. For the bathtub fall call, why is it still important to write the report in a narrative format rather than relying on check boxes alone?

choices: Speak slowly, clearly, and distinctly, allow her enough time to comprehend and respond, and make sure she has her eyeglasses or hearing aids if she uses them
Speak louder and faster so she can keep up with what you are doing
Have the hospice worker answer your questions on her behalf
Use precise medical terminology so nothing is lost in translation
questions.explanation: As the sender of information, you adjust to the receiver: slow, clear speech, time to process and answer, and the patient's assistive devices in place — or an interpreter when needed. Volume and speed, speaking through someone else, and jargon all increase the chance of being misunderstood.
questions.question: The 86-year-old woman has been sitting in a cold bathtub for hours, she is hard to understand when she is upset, and like many patients her age she may rely on eyeglasses or hearing aids that are not on her right now. What best minimizes miscommunication with her?

choices: Promise her the collar will come off within five minutes so she calms down
Tell her it will definitely come off as soon as you reach the ambulance
Decline to discuss it and tell her the hospital will explain everything
Tell her honestly that you do not know, and explain it will depend on how long the hospital staff need to assess her injuries
questions.explanation: "I don't know" is an acceptable answer when it is the truth — paired with what will actually determine the answer, which is the hospital's assessment. Invented times or refusals to answer break the trust you have been building with her.
questions.question: The woman cannot stand the c-collar. Immobilized on the gurney and frightened of falling, she asks you directly how long she has to wear the collar and lie flat. You honestly do not know. How should you answer her?

choices: It is acceptable, because keeping her calm is the priority
Deception can destroy the patient's trust in you — direct questions should get honest answers, even if you do not share every detail
It is acceptable as long as the time you make up turns out to be close
It only becomes a problem if she later finds out it was not true
questions.explanation: Misinforming a patient to buy temporary calm is not justifiable: when the promise proves false, her trust in you — and in the next crew — is damaged. Honest answers, reassurance, and validating her concerns reduce anxiety without lying to her.
questions.question: Your partner quietly suggests telling the woman the collar "comes off in five minutes" just to lower her anxiety on the ride, even though neither of you knows that. What is the problem with that approach?
